request.q: Hot water burned my arm and my sleeve is stuck to the skin. Should I pull it off?

results.answer:
**Local passages supplied.** They may not support every part of this answer; citations are not independently verified.

**Generated answer withheld.** A citation or action-condition check failed. Consult the original references below and seek qualified help. These checks do not establish medical accuracy or verify every claim.



**Source-backed fallback guidance**

The generated answer is unavailable. These steps come from the versioned references shown below; follow their stated conditions.

For a thermal burn, cool the area under cool running water for 20 minutes while keeping the rest of the person warm [2]. Remove nearby clothing and jewelry only if not stuck to the skin [2]. Do not apply ice, butter or oils, or burst blisters [2]. After cooling, lay clean cling film loosely over the burn; do not wrap it around a limb or put it on the face [2]. Seek emergency care for large, deep burns or burns on the face or genitals; seek medical advice if unsure [2].

> ⚠️ First-aid guidance only; it does not replace medical care. If help is available, seek it.

sources.text:
1. Move away from the heat source. If clothing catches fire: **stop, drop and roll**.
2. **Cool with cool (not ice-cold) running water for at least 20 minutes** — this still helps up to 3 hours after the burn.
3. Remove rings, watches and clothing that isn't stuck before swelling sets in.
4. Cover with **kitchen plastic wrap** (in layers, not wrapped tightly) or a clean, damp cloth.
5. **Do not use** ice, butter, toothpaste, coffee grounds, oil. Do not pop blisters.
6. Prevent hypothermia: cool the burn, but keep the rest of the body warm.
7. Offer fluids if the person is conscious.

**Seek medical care** if: larger than the victim's palm, deep (white, brown, painless), on the face, hands, feet, genitals, joints, electrical or chemical burn, smoke inhalation (hoarseness, soot in the nose), or in children and elderly people.

**Chemical:** remove contaminated clothing and rinse with plenty of running water for 20 minutes or more. Dry powder: brush off before rinsing.

> Source: IFRC 2020; British Burns Association — First Aid Clinical Practice Guidelines (2018); Sociedade Brasileira de Queimaduras (Brazilian Burns Society).

sources.title: Burn
sources.text:
Burn patients require support and care – both physiological and psychological. Respiratory failure, sepsis, and multi-organ system failure are common in hospitalized burn patients. To prevent hypothermia and maintain normal body temperature, burn patients with over 20% of burn injuries should be kept in an environment with the temperature at or above 30 degree Celsius.[90]

Metabolism in burn patients proceeds at a higher than normal speed due to the whole-body process and rapid fatty acid substrate cycles, which can be countered with an adequate supply of energy, nutrients, and antioxidants. Enteral feeding a day after resuscitation is required to reduce risk of infection, recovery time, non-infectious complications, hospital stay, long-term damage, and mortality. Controlling blood glucose levels can have an impact on liver function and survival.

Risk of thromboembolism is high and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) that does not resolve with maximal ventilator use is also a common complication. Scars are long-term after-effects of a burn injury. Psychological support is required to cope with the aftermath of a fire accident, while to prevent scars and long-term damage to the skin and other body structures consulting with burn specialists, preventing infections, consuming nutritious foods, early and aggressive rehabilitation, and using compressive clothing are recommended.

request.q: Me quemé el brazo y la ropa está pegada a la piel. ¿Debo quitarla?

results.answer:
**Fragmentos locales proporcionados.** Puede que no respalden toda la respuesta; las citas no se han verificado de forma independiente.

**Respuesta generada retenida.** Falló una comprobación de citas o de las condiciones de una acción. Consulte las referencias originales a continuación y busque ayuda cualificada. Estas comprobaciones no garantizan la exactitud médica ni verifican todas las afirmaciones.



**Orientación alternativa basada en fuentes**

La respuesta generada no está disponible. Estos pasos proceden de las referencias versionadas que aparecen abajo; respete sus condiciones.

Para una quemadura térmica, enfríe la zona con agua corriente fresca durante 20 minutos, manteniendo el resto del cuerpo caliente [2]. Retire ropa y joyas cercanas solo si no están pegadas a la piel [2]. No aplique hielo, mantequilla ni aceites, ni reviente ampollas [2]. Después de enfriar, coloque film plástico limpio y suelto sobre la quemadura; no envuelva la extremidad ni lo coloque en la cara [2]. Busque urgencias para quemaduras grandes, profundas, en la cara o genitales; consulte si tiene dudas [2].

sources.doc_title: Primeros auxilios y cuidados de salud
sources.text:
1. Aleje a la persona de la fuente de calor. Si la ropa se prende fuego: **deténgase, tírese al suelo y ruede**.
2. **Enfríe con agua corriente fría (no helada) durante al menos 20 minutos** — sirve hasta 3 horas después de la quemadura.
3. Retire anillos, relojes y ropa no adherida antes de que se hinche.
4. Cubra con **film plástico de cocina** (en capas, sin envolver apretado) o un paño limpio y húmedo.
5. **No use** hielo, mantequilla, pasta de dientes, borra de café ni aceite. No reviente las ampollas.
6. Prevenga la hipotermia: enfríe la quemadura, pero mantenga abrigado el resto del cuerpo.
7. Ofrezca líquidos si la persona está consciente.

**Busque atención** si: es mayor que la palma de la mano de la víctima, profunda (blanca, marrón, sin dolor), en la cara, manos, pies, genitales, articulaciones, quemadura eléctrica o química, por inhalación de humo (ronquera, hollín en la nariz), o en niños y adultos mayores.

**Química:** retire la ropa contaminada y lave con mucha agua corriente durante 20 minutos o más. Polvo seco: cepíllelo antes de lavar.

> Fuente: IFRC 2020; British Burns Association — First Aid Clinical Practice Guidelines (2018); Sociedade Brasileira de Queimaduras.

sources.title: Electrical burn
sources.text: An electrically burned patient should not be touched or treated until the source of electricity has been removed.[12] Electrical injuries often extend beyond burns and include cardiac arrhythmia, such as ventricular fibrillation. First aid treatments include assessment of consciousness of the victim, evaluation of pulse and circulation, and treatment of burns.[15]

For a thermal burn, cool the area under cool running water for 20 minutes while keeping the rest of the person warm [2]. Remove nearby clothing and jewelry only if not stuck to the skin [2]. sources.text:
1. Move away from the heat source. If clothing catches fire: **stop, drop and roll**.
2. **Cool with cool (not ice-cold) running water for at least 20 minutes** — this still helps up to 3 hours after the burn.
3. Remove rings, watches and clothing that isn't stuck before swelling sets in.
4. Cover with **kitchen plastic wrap** (in layers, not wrapped tightly) or a clean, damp cloth.
5. **Do not use** ice, butter, toothpaste, coffee grounds, oil. Do not pop blisters.
6. Prevent hypothermia: cool the burn, but keep the rest of the body warm.
7. Offer fluids if the person is conscious.

**Seek medical care** if: larger than the victim's palm, deep (white, brown, painless), on the face, hands, feet, genitals, joints, electrical or chemical burn, smoke inhalation (hoarseness, soot in the nose), or in children and elderly people.

**Chemical:** remove contaminated clothing and rinse with plenty of running water for 20 minutes or more. Dry powder: brush off before rinsing.

> Source: IFRC 2020; British Burns Association — First Aid Clinical Practice Guidelines (2018); Sociedade Brasileira de Queimaduras (Brazilian Burns Society).

sources.title: Burn
sources.text:
Burn patients require support and care – both physiological and psychological. Respiratory failure, sepsis, and multi-organ system failure are common in hospitalized burn patients. To prevent hypothermia and maintain normal body temperature, burn patients with over 20% of burn injuries should be kept in an environment with the temperature at or above 30 degree Celsius.[90]

Metabolism in burn patients proceeds at a higher than normal speed due to the whole-body process and rapid fatty acid substrate cycles, which can be countered with an adequate supply of energy, nutrients, and antioxidants. Enteral feeding a day after resuscitation is required to reduce risk of infection, recovery time, non-infectious complications, hospital stay, long-term damage, and mortality. Controlling blood glucose levels can have an impact on liver function and survival.

Risk of thromboembolism is high and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) that does not resolve with maximal ventilator use is also a common complication. Scars are long-term after-effects of a burn injury. Psychological support is required to cope with the aftermath of a fire accident, while to prevent scars and long-term damage to the skin and other body structures consulting with burn specialists, preventing infections, consuming nutritious foods, early and aggressive rehabilitation, and using compressive clothing are recommended.

sources.text:
1. Aleje a la persona de la fuente de calor. Si la ropa se prende fuego: **deténgase, tírese al suelo y ruede**.
2. **Enfríe con agua corriente fría (no helada) durante al menos 20 minutos** — sirve hasta 3 horas después de la quemadura.
3. Retire anillos, relojes y ropa no adherida antes de que se hinche.
4. Cubra con **film plástico de cocina** (en capas, sin envolver apretado) o un paño limpio y húmedo.
5. **No use** hielo, mantequilla, pasta de dientes, borra de café ni aceite. No reviente las ampollas.
6. Prevenga la hipotermia: enfríe la quemadura, pero mantenga abrigado el resto del cuerpo.
7. Ofrezca líquidos si la persona está consciente.
